catalog_quote: As a rule, the last syllable of a Turkmen word is stressed. However, particles and certain suffixes added to the ends of words are not stressed.

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations are verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated places (Tyson & Clark 1993 p. 8; Gray 2004 sec. 2.4 p. 7), and a second open Peace Corps volume downloaded now (ERIC ED358743, p. 8) repeats the same statement. The classification (fixed final stress, word domain, with certain suffixes/particles unstressed) matches every description seen and StressTyp2. The weakness is source tier: a Peace Corps manual and a 32-pp SIL sketch, while the 708-pp Clark 1998 reference grammar (which Gray explicitly defers to at pp. 79ff) and the 2021 Routledge chapter are unheld. Nothing suggests the classification would change; a re-read of Clark 1998:79ff would upgrade the citation and pin down the exception list (pre-stressing -mi, negative/copular clitics etc.), which matters for the 'strict' flag but not the dominant-final classification.

sources.quote: Stress is usually on the last syllable of the root, when pronounced in isolation. It is easy for mother-tongue English speakers to confuse stress and length e.g. bägül [bä:'gül] – rose – has an unstressed lengthened first syllable and a short, but stressed, second syllable. Avoid saying ['bä:gül], which might be misunderstood. With the addition of affixes of any kind, the stress is on the last syllable, except in the case of words with the question particle –mi, the plural imperative marker –yň/iň and one or two other affixes.
sources.note: Held copy: archive.org item 032-turkmen (held_mirror/source_audit_2026-09-16/turk1304/ per, byte-identical to morphstress_f2/turk1304/; text, sec. 2.4 at lines 269-284, printed p. 7 = PDF p. 7 of 32). Read in full for this record (the entry's exception quotation is this passage). Gray states final stress on the root and on affixed words and names the unstressed affixes (question particle -mi, plural imperative -yň/iň, 'one or two other affixes'), with the contrast pairs garawul gara'wul / garawuldan garawul'dan.. barmak bar'mak / baryň! 'baryň; the entry's own quotation (Tyson & Clark 1993: 'particles and certain suffixes') leaves them unnamed. Footnote 3 printed at the foot of p. 7 ('For futher information see Clark:98:79f who describes how this works out in practice for the largest tribe, the Teke') is keyed to sec. 2.3 Vowel Harmony ('..corresponding spoken forms, which vary from dialect to dialect3'), not to the stress paragraph, which carries no citation: the stress statement is Gray's own (SIL-NEG sketch, David Gray 1994, edited May 1999 / May 2001 / June 2004, file header 16/12/2011). Same work as the 'Primary: Gray, David. 1994/2004' morphology-study row (row 4), which bears nothing and is not counted twice.
